idiom_name: generic Range[T cmp.Ordered] struct with Contains/Overlaps methods
implementation_notes: Go has no interval type: range is a loop keyword over slices, maps and channels, not a value, and the standard library offers only primitive comparison. Since Go 1.18 the classic structure is cheap to write properly - a struct parameterised by cmp.Ordered whose methods compare with cmp.Compare, which covers ints, floats, strings and time.Time - so the pattern costs one small type instead of an interface hierarchy. Open ends need *T endpoints (nil meaning unbounded) or an explicit flag, because Go has no Option type; third-party generic interval packages exist (die-net/intervals for half-open ranges that merge on insert, mokeko/interval for bound kinds) but none is dominant, so the hand-written struct remains the norm for a single domain type.
pitfalls: A nil *T endpoint means 'unbounded', but the zero value of T (time.Time{}, 0) is a legitimate endpoint: mixing pointer and value endpoints in one struct makes Contains panic or compare against the wrong thing.

cmp.Compare gives floats a total order in which NaN sorts below everything, so an interval with a NaN endpoint contains values that IEEE-754 comparison would reject - validate endpoints when the domain is numeric.
Value receivers (Range[T], not *Range[T]) keep the interval copyable and usable as a map key; a pointer receiver makes the type non-comparable for maps and invites accidental mutation.
time.Time comparisons are wall-clock aware: cmp.Compare uses the monotonic reading when both operands have one, so a range built from time.Now() and one parsed from text can compare inconsistently.
